events.title: Great Fire of London
events.blurb: A blaze beginning in a baker's shop on Pudding Lane burned for four days, destroying 373 acres of the medieval city including 13,200 houses, 87 churches, and most civic buildings. The fire melted the lead roof of St. Paul's Cathedral and was visible 60 miles away, yet officially killed only six people due to rapid evacuation before the flames spread.

events.title: Mount Tambora Eruption
events.blurb: A volcano on an Indonesian island blew its top in the most powerful eruption in recorded history, spewing 150 cubic kilometres of material into the atmosphere. The sulphate aerosols lingered in the stratosphere for years, cooling global temperatures by roughly a degree and producing crop failures, famine, and snow in June across the northern hemisphere the following year.
events.revealBlurb: April 10, 1815 — Mount Tambora on Sumbawa, Indonesia. 1816 became "the year without a summer." Mary Shelley, trapped indoors by endless rain in Switzerland, wrote Frankenstein. J.M.W. Turner's lurid sunsets from the decade owe their color to Tambora's dust.

events.title: Krakatoa Eruption
events.blurb: An island volcano in the strait between two large Indonesian islands exploded in a series of detonations culminating in a final blast so loud it was heard 4,800 kilometres away and circled the planet four times as a pressure wave. The eruption generated tsunamis that killed 36,000 people on surrounding coasts; the resulting atmospheric dust produced red-green sunsets worldwide for years.
events.revealBlurb: August 27, 1883 — Krakatoa, Sunda Strait. The final explosion had an acoustic energy roughly equivalent to 200 megatons of TNT. The glow of the afterburn may be what Edvard Munch painted in The Scream a decade later.

events.title: San Francisco Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.9 earthquake ripped a 477-kilometre tear through the fault running up the California coast, hitting a West Coast boom city just after 5 AM. The shaking was severe, but the four-day fire that followed — fed by broken gas mains and fought with limited water from shattered pipes — did most of the damage, destroying 80 percent of the city and killing around 3,000.
events.revealBlurb: April 18, 1906 — San Francisco. The mayor authorized dynamiting buildings to create firebreaks; most of the dynamiting actually spread the fire. The opera singer Enrico Caruso, in town for a performance, vowed never to return. He didn't.

events.title: Mount St. Helens Eruption
events.blurb: A Pacific Northwest volcano that had been swelling a grotesque 150-metre bulge on its north flank for two months underwent a catastrophic lateral blast triggered by an earthquake. The collapse produced the largest landslide in recorded history, flattening 600 square kilometres of forest and killing 57 people, including a stubborn innkeeper who refused to evacuate.
events.revealBlurb: May 18, 1980 — Washington State, USA. The innkeeper was Harry R. Truman, 83, who kept pets and a collection of bourbon at his lodge and became a folk hero for his refusal to leave. His body was never found.

events.title: First Public Film Screening
events.blurb: Two French brothers, sons of a portrait photographer, held the first commercial screening of projected motion pictures in the basement of a Paris café. The audience of 33 paid one franc each to watch ten short films — workers leaving a factory, a baby being fed, a boat leaving a harbor. Their cinematograph was both camera and projector; the film was 35mm. Within a year their operators were touring every continent.
events.revealBlurb: December 28, 1895 — Louis and Auguste Lumière at the Salon Indien du Grand Café, Paris. The apocryphal story that audiences ran screaming from the train-arriving film comes from a later screening. The Lumières thought cinema was "an invention without a future" and quickly moved on to other projects.

events.title: Citizen Kane Released
events.blurb: A 25-year-old radio and theatre prodigy made his feature film directing debut with a quasi-biographical study of a newspaper tycoon, structurally organized as a series of flashback interviews about the man's last word ("Rosebud"). The film used deep-focus cinematography, low-angle setups, overlapping dialogue, and non-linear structure in ways that rewrote the cinematic grammar of the next 70 years. Its real-life subject, a media baron, tried to have every print destroyed.
events.revealBlurb: May 1, 1941 — Orson Welles, age 25. The target was William Randolph Hearst, who banned mention of the film in his newspapers. It lost Best Picture to "How Green Was My Valley." It tops nearly every "greatest films of all time" list.

events.title: Jaws Released
events.blurb: A 28-year-old director released a 124-minute thriller about a great white shark terrorizing a New England beach resort. Principal photography, supposed to last 55 days, ran 159; the mechanical shark broke down constantly and was rarely shown, producing the film's signature off-screen menace. Released across a record number of screens nationwide with a saturation TV ad campaign, it invented the summer blockbuster.
events.revealBlurb: June 20, 1975 — Steven Spielberg. The shark's malfunctions forced Spielberg to rely on John Williams' two-note score to telegraph the threat. The film caused a measurable drop in US beach attendance for years afterward.

events.title: Star Wars Released
events.blurb: A 33-year-old American director released a science-fiction film mashing up elements of samurai cinema, WWII dogfight pictures, and Joseph Campbell's monomyth theory, with groundbreaking effects assembled in a repurposed warehouse with a workforce assembled from scratch. The studio had cut his budget and expected the film to flop; one executive had retitled it "The Adventures of Luke Starkiller." Lines began forming at theatres on opening morning and did not stop for years.
events.revealBlurb: May 25, 1977 — George Lucas. He traded his directing salary for merchandising rights; he became a billionaire. The effects company he had to build from scratch, Industrial Light & Magic, became the industry standard for decades. Campbell wept watching the film.

events.title: Toy Story Released
events.blurb: A California animation studio released the first feature film produced entirely with computer-generated imagery, a 81-minute buddy comedy about a child's cowboy doll who feels threatened by a new space-ranger action figure. The studio had spent four years on the film, through three near-cancellations and total rewrites; the resulting picture grossed $390 million and established a new production studio as the dominant force in animation for the next two decades.
events.revealBlurb: November 22, 1995 — Pixar Animation Studios, directed by John Lasseter. Tom Hanks and Tim Allen voiced Woody and Buzz Lightyear. Pixar had been Apple founder Steve Jobs's expensive side-project; Disney bought them for $7.4 billion in 2006.

events.title: First Smallpox Vaccination
events.blurb: An English country doctor inoculated a healthy eight-year-old boy with material extracted from a milkmaid's cowpox blister, then six weeks later deliberately exposed the child to smallpox. When the boy showed no symptoms, the physician had demonstrated that a mild related disease could confer immunity against a deadly one — founding the practice of vaccination.

events.title: Pasteur's Rabies Vaccine Used on a Human
events.blurb: A French chemist administered the first human dose of an experimental rabies treatment to a nine-year-old boy who had been severely bitten by a rabid dog two days earlier and faced certain death without intervention. The boy survived, and the successful case launched the practice of post-exposure vaccination for infectious disease.

events.title: Insulin Administered to a Patient
events.blurb: A 14-year-old diabetic patient near death at a Toronto hospital received an injection of pancreatic extract prepared by two medical researchers after earlier formulations had failed due to impurities. The boy recovered, and researchers moved ward to ward injecting the remaining diabetic patients — transforming a death sentence into a manageable condition within weeks.

events.title: First Human Heart Transplant
events.blurb: A South African surgeon transplanted the heart of a 25-year-old accident victim into a 53-year-old grocer in a nine-hour operation at Groote Schuur Hospital in Cape Town. The recipient survived 18 days before dying of pneumonia; the same surgical team performed a second transplant 13 days later — that patient lived 19 months.

events.title: WHO Certifies Smallpox Eradication
events.blurb: The World Health Assembly certified the global eradication of smallpox — the only human infectious disease ever deliberately driven to extinction — following a 13-year WHO campaign using ring vaccination to contain and eliminate every remaining outbreak. The last naturally occurring case had been recorded in Somalia in 1977, ending a disease that had killed an estimated 300 million people in the 20th century alone.

events.title: Don Giovanni Premieres
events.blurb: A 31-year-old composer conducted the premiere of his two-act opera about a dissolute nobleman's pursuit of women and eventual descent into Hell, before Prague nobility at the Estates Theatre. According to his librettist, the overture was composed the night before the premiere while the composer's wife kept him awake through the small hours with punch and fairy tales.

events.title: Beethoven's 9th Symphony Premieres
events.blurb: A completely deaf composer conducted the premiere of a 65-minute choral symphony in Vienna, his back turned to the audience so he could follow the orchestral score. When the work ended, a soprano soloist had to turn him around to witness the five-round standing ovation — he could hear nothing of the applause that shook the hall.

events.title: Elvis Records "That's All Right"
events.blurb: During a break in a fruitless recording session in Memphis, a 19-year-old truck driver began playing an uptempo blues song with such energy that the studio owner halted the session, rewound the tape, and asked him to do it again from the start. The recording blended country and rhythm-and-blues in a style that had no existing commercial category.

events.title: Woodstock Festival Opens
events.blurb: A music festival on a dairy farm in upstate New York that had sold 186,000 advance tickets was overwhelmed by more than 400,000 attendees in the preceding 48 hours, forcing organisers to declare it a free event and abandon the ticket booths. Thirty-two acts performed over four rain-soaked days, and the festival became the defining cultural gathering of its generation.

events.title: Beatles' Final Public Performance
events.blurb: A four-piece rock band performed without announcement on the roof of their recording company's London headquarters for 42 minutes in near-freezing winter temperatures, drawing a crowd of hundreds in the street below before police ended the show citing noise complaints. The impromptu rooftop set was their last performance together in front of a live audience.

events.title: Battle of Salamis
events.blurb: A Greek allied fleet of roughly 370 triremes, lured into position by a false message from the Athenian commander, engaged a Persian fleet of perhaps 800 in the narrow straits between a small island and the Athenian mainland coast. The Persian ships, crowded in the strait, could not maneuver; the Greek triremes rammed them methodically for twelve hours. Over 200 Persian ships were sunk or captured. The Persian king watched the disaster unfold from a throne on the adjacent mainland.
events.revealBlurb: September 480 BCE — Themistocles, Athenian strategos. The Persian king was Xerxes I; he retreated to Asia with much of his army, leaving a smaller force that was destroyed at Plataea the following year. Aeschylus, who had fought at Salamis himself, wrote a play about it eight years later.

events.title: Qin Shi Huang Unifies China
events.blurb: A 38-year-old king of a northwestern Chinese state, having conquered the other six rival warring states over a decade of campaigning, declared himself "First Emperor" of a unified Chinese empire. He standardized weights, measures, currency, and written script across his new realm; built a system of roads and canals; and began construction of the infrastructure that would become the Great Wall. His dynasty collapsed within four years of his death; his successor dynasty, the Han, would last four centuries.
events.revealBlurb: 221 BCE — Qin Shi Huang (Ying Zheng). He was obsessed with immortality; some scholars believe the mercury he consumed as an "elixir" hastened his death in 210 BCE. His 8,000-figure terracotta-army tomb, excavated from 1974 on, is his most famous monument. China is named for the Qin.

events.title: Julius Caesar Assassinated
events.blurb: A Roman dictator, having been named dictator-for-life a month earlier, was stabbed 23 times by a group of 60 senators at a meeting of the Senate held in a Pompey-built theatre. The assassins, styling themselves "Liberators," had convinced themselves that removing the man who had effectively ended the Republic would restore it. Instead, his death plunged Rome into 14 more years of civil war, at the end of which his adopted heir emerged as the first Roman emperor in all but name.
events.revealBlurb: March 15, 44 BCE — the Ides of March. Conspirators included Brutus and Cassius. The supposed last words "Et tu, Brute?" come from Shakespeare; Caesar's actual last words — if he spoke any — may have been the Greek "kai su, teknon?" ("you too, my child?"). His heir Octavian defeated the conspirators at Philippi two years later.

events.title: Hadrian's Wall Begun
events.blurb: A Roman emperor, touring his empire's northern frontier in Britannia, ordered the construction of a 117-kilometre stone-and-turf fortification across the narrow neck of the island from coast to coast. Sixteen forts and dozens of smaller milecastles were strung along it, garrisoned by auxiliary troops from across the empire. It was less a continuous fighting wall than a filter — controlling movement, collecting customs, and projecting imperial authority. Much of it still stands; the wall defined the political frontier for three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: 122 CE — Emperor Hadrian. Construction took six years and employed three legions. Hadrian himself famously declared at the start of his reign that Rome would not continue to expand its borders indefinitely — reversing his predecessor Trajan's conquests in Mesopotamia.

events.title: Dedication of Constantinople
events.blurb: Constantine ceremonially dedicated his rebuilt city on the Bosphorus — built on the site of the old Greek colony of Byzantium — as Nova Roma, "New Rome," after six years of construction. The city was positioned to control trade routes between Europe and Asia, had natural defences on three sides, and was explicitly Christian in character, with no traditional pagan temples.
events.revealBlurb: May 11, 330 CE. Constantine commissioned a massive porphyry column topped with a statue of himself as Apollo-Sol to stand at the city's centre. Legends later claimed he buried holy Christian relics in its base. The column still stands in Istanbul, badly scorched but intact, called Cemberlitas.

events.title: Pont du Gard Built
events.blurb: A three-tiered limestone aqueduct bridge was constructed to carry water 50 kilometres across southern Gaul to the Roman colony of Nemausus (modern Nîmes). The top level — 48 metres above the River Gard — still carried its channel; the whole structure spans 275 metres. It was built dry, without mortar, using stones so precisely cut that the joints remain watertight after two millennia. The aqueduct itself was decommissioned in the 6th century; the bridge survived as a road crossing.
events.revealBlurb: c. 50 CE — built under Emperor Claudius. The water it carried had a gradient of only 1 in 3,000 — about 30 centimetres of drop per kilometre. The Pont du Gard is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most visited tourist destinations in France.

events.title: Pantheon of Rome Completed
events.blurb: A Roman emperor completed a rebuilt temple, topped with an unreinforced concrete dome 43.3 metres in diameter — the largest dome in the world for over 1,300 years, and still the largest unreinforced-concrete dome ever built. A 9-metre oculus at its apex is the only source of natural light. The dome's concrete mix grew lighter toward the top (using pumice aggregate), and its coffered interior thinned as it rose, reducing weight where it mattered.
events.revealBlurb: c. 126 CE — Emperor Hadrian, rebuilding an earlier Agrippa temple destroyed by fire. It became a Catholic church in 609 CE, which is why it survived intact unlike other Roman temples. Raphael and the Italian kings Victor Emmanuel II and Umberto I are buried inside.

events.title: Notre-Dame de Paris Completed
events.blurb: The main fabric of a Gothic cathedral on an island in the Seine at the heart of the French capital was finished after 182 years of construction. Its twin western towers, flying buttresses, three great rose windows, and vast nave became the template for French Gothic architecture. It survived the Wars of Religion, the French Revolution (when it was briefly rededicated to a "Cult of Reason"), Haussmann's 19th-century restorations, and two world wars — before a fire in 2019 collapsed its 19th-century spire and much of its roof.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1345 — Notre-Dame cathedral, Paris. Construction began in 1163. The 19th-century restoration was led by Eugène Viollet-le-Duc. The 2019 fire's cause was never conclusively determined; reconstruction was completed in December 2024.

events.title: Brooklyn Bridge Opens
events.blurb: The longest suspension bridge in the world — 486 metres between its Gothic granite towers — opened to foot and carriage traffic linking Manhattan and Brooklyn across the East River. Its construction had taken 14 years and cost 27 lives. The chief engineer had been paralyzed by decompression sickness while supervising caisson work; his wife Emily had effectively managed the final decade of the project from notes dictated in his sickroom.
events.revealBlurb: May 24, 1883 — designed by John A. Roebling (who died from a dockside accident early in construction). His son Washington Roebling suffered caisson disease and was bedridden; daughter-in-law Emily Warren Roebling led onsite engineering management. She was the first person to cross the completed bridge, in a carriage carrying a rooster.

events.title: Empire State Building Opens
events.blurb: A 381-metre, 102-story skyscraper opened in Manhattan, having been designed in two weeks and constructed in just 410 days — often at a rate of 4.5 stories per week. It displaced the Chrysler Building as the tallest building in the world and held that title for 41 years. The Great Depression left it mostly empty for its first decade; New Yorkers nicknamed it the "Empty State Building." It entered profit in 1950.
events.revealBlurb: May 1, 1931 — architect William F. Lamb (Shreve, Lamb and Harmon). The B-25 bomber that crashed into the 79th floor in heavy fog on July 28, 1945 killed 14 people but damaged the structure only moderately. King Kong famously climbed it in the 1933 film.

events.title: Beethoven's Ninth Premieres
events.blurb: A nearly deaf 53-year-old composer, standing on the podium while a co-conductor did the actual directing, premiered a vast hour-long symphony that broke with convention by adding four vocal soloists and a chorus to the orchestra in its final movement. The text was a Schiller poem celebrating universal brotherhood. At the end the composer had to be turned around by one of the singers to see the audience — which he otherwise could not hear — thundering applause.
events.revealBlurb: May 7, 1824 — Ludwig van Beethoven at the Theater am Kärntnertor, Vienna. He had been profoundly deaf for over a decade. The "Ode to Joy" theme is now, somewhat jarringly given the text, the official anthem of the European Union.

events.title: Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake Premieres
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Russian composer's first full-length ballet score premiered at a grand theatre in the Russian capital, paired with choreography that was widely thought incompetent and dancing that was widely thought under-rehearsed. Critics focused their complaints on the music, which they found too "symphonic" for dancing. Only after the composer's death, in a restaged 1895 version with new choreography, did the ballet become a classic.
events.revealBlurb: March 4, 1877 — Pyotr Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake at the Bolshoi, Moscow (Old Style February 20). The 1895 St. Petersburg revival with Petipa/Ivanov choreography is the version most companies perform today. The tragic black-swan finale was a 1950s restoration.

events.title: Elvis's First Sun Session
events.blurb: A 19-year-old truck driver who had walked into a small Memphis recording studio a year earlier to make an acetate for his mother's birthday showed up for a late-night try-out with two local session musicians. The session was going nowhere until, during a break, the kid started goofing around with an old R&B song by Arthur Crudup. The engineer slapped the tape on and caught it. Within weeks the song was a regional hit.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1954 — Elvis Presley, Scotty Moore, and Bill Black at Sun Records, Memphis. The song was "That's All Right (Mama)." Studio owner Sam Phillips had famously said he could make "a billion dollars" if he could find a white man who sang with a Black feel.

events.title: Dylan Goes Electric
events.blurb: A 24-year-old folk singer, backed by a ragged rhythm section from the previous night's acquaintance, walked onto the stage of a folk festival on a Rhode Island pier with a sunburst Stratocaster slung low over his shoulder. He played three short electric songs before some boos drowned out the applause. He walked off, returned with his acoustic, and played two more. The event marked, depending on who tells it, the birth of folk-rock or the betrayal of American folk.
events.revealBlurb: July 25, 1965 — Bob Dylan at the Newport Folk Festival. Pete Seeger, legend says, tried to cut the sound cables with an axe. Seeger later denied it. The songs included "Maggie's Farm" and "Like a Rolling Stone." Dylan's next tour was booed nightly for a year.

events.title: Paul Simon's Graceland Released
events.blurb: A 44-year-old American songwriter released an album recorded largely in Johannesburg studios with South African musicians, fusing American folk and pop with mbaqanga, isicathamiya, and zydeco. The album was controversial: the United Nations had called for a cultural boycott of the apartheid regime, and many considered the recording sessions a violation. The finished record was nonetheless a critical and commercial phenomenon and was credited with exposing mass audiences to South African musical traditions.
events.revealBlurb: August 25, 1986 — Paul Simon. Collaborators included Ladysmith Black Mambazo, Ray Phiri, and the Boyoyo Boys. Simon was blacklisted by the UN but sang in Zimbabwe and Zambia; Nelson Mandela later thanked him for the cultural bridge.

events.title: First Iron Bridge Opens
events.blurb: A cast-iron arch bridge opened across a gorge of the Severn River in western England, the first substantial bridge anywhere in the world constructed entirely of iron. Its five parallel ribs, each cast as a single 21-metre piece, spanned 30 metres and weighed 384 tonnes. The bridge was built partly as a structural demonstration by a local ironmaster promoting the capabilities of his foundries.
events.revealBlurb: January 1, 1781 — Ironbridge, Shropshire. Designer Thomas Farnolls Pritchard, ironmaster Abraham Darby III. It still stands as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The surrounding gorge is considered the cradle of the Industrial Revolution.

events.title: Cotton Gin Patented
events.blurb: A 28-year-old Yale-educated New Englander, tutoring at a Georgia plantation, built a simple wooden cylinder with wire teeth that combed cotton seeds out of fibres 50 times faster than a slave's fingers could. He patented the device. Rather than being royally enriched, he spent years litigating piracy; the design was too simple to protect. The invention made short-staple cotton profitable across the American South, entrenching slavery economically just as it was weakening elsewhere.
events.revealBlurb: March 14, 1794 — Eli Whitney. He later pivoted to manufacturing muskets with interchangeable parts — an innovation that shaped the later assembly-line system. Demand for enslaved labour in the Deep South grew enormously between 1790 and 1860, in large part because of the gin.

events.title: US Transcontinental Railroad Completed
events.blurb: Officials drove a ceremonial golden spike into a rail tie at a desolate spot in Utah, joining rails built eastward from Sacramento by Chinese labourers and rails built westward from the Missouri River by Irish labourers. Travel from New York to San Francisco, previously a six-month journey by wagon or ship, now took a week. The two companies, a state-subsidized joint venture, had raced each other for six years; the route had been set by the Lincoln administration in 1862.
events.revealBlurb: May 10, 1869 — Promontory Summit, Utah. The joining rails were two: Central Pacific from the west, Union Pacific from the east. The spike ceremony was telegraphed to the rest of the country; the "Done" message was the first cross-country news bulletin. The Chinese workers who had done most of the hardest labour were not invited to the ceremony.

events.title: Coca-Cola Invented
events.blurb: An Atlanta pharmacist, a former Confederate officer who had become addicted to morphine following a Civil War injury, mixed a flavoured syrup of coca leaves and kola nuts with carbonated water at a downtown soda fountain and began selling it by the glass as a "brain tonic." The formula initially contained a small amount of cocaine; it was removed in 1903. The modestly popular local beverage grew into the world's most recognized consumer brand.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1886 — John Pemberton at Jacobs' Pharmacy, Atlanta. Pemberton sold the formula piecemeal in ill health; Asa Griggs Candler consolidated ownership and built the business. Coca-Cola's secret recipe, "Merchandise 7X," is supposedly known to only two executives at any time.

events.title: Wright Brothers' First Flight
events.blurb: Two American bicycle-shop owners from Dayton, Ohio achieved the first sustained, controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air aircraft on a windswept dune at the Outer Banks of North Carolina. The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 36 metres — about the wingspan of a modern commercial airliner. They made three more flights that morning; the fourth covered 260 metres in 59 seconds. Few newspapers reported the achievement; commercial aviation took another three decades to arrive.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1903 — Orville and Wilbur Wright at Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, NC. The flyer is now in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum. The pair spent 4 years after their first flight battling patent disputes and litigation rather than manufacturing planes.

events.title: Women's March on Versailles
events.blurb: Around 7,000 Parisian market women, enraged by the soaring price of bread, armed themselves with kitchen knives and broomsticks and marched 20 kilometres in a cold autumn rain to the royal palace. The crowd invaded the queen's bedchamber; the royal family was compelled to return to the capital under escort the next morning and never saw the palace again.
events.revealBlurb: October 5, 1789 — early French Revolution. The queen escaped through a connecting corridor. Lafayette, commanding the citizen-militia National Guard, rode in circles trying to maintain order. Within two years, Marie Antoinette would be in a cell.

events.title: FDA Approves the Pill
events.blurb: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved a daily oral contraceptive pill combining synthetic estrogen and progestin for sale as a birth-control product, two years after approving the same drug for menstrual disorders. Over two million American women were taking it within three years. It was the first drug ever developed for use by healthy people rather than sick ones, and it reshaped women's labour-force participation for the next half-century.
events.revealBlurb: May 9, 1960 — Enovid, made by G.D. Searle. The research had been funded privately by heiress Katharine McCormick because federal funding was politically impossible. Single women could be denied prescriptions until a 1972 Supreme Court ruling.

events.title: The Feminine Mystique Published
events.blurb: A former labour journalist who had been writing articles for women's magazines published a 410-page book analyzing what she called "the problem that has no name" — the stifling dissatisfaction of educated suburban housewives. It sold three million copies within three years and became the foundational text of a resurgent American feminist movement that would transform employment law, education policy, and reproductive rights.
events.revealBlurb: February 19, 1963 — Betty Friedan. The book drew on her research into a Smith College alumni survey. Friedan went on to co-found the National Organization for Women in 1966 and help lead the 1970 Women's Strike for Equality.

events.title: Margaret Thatcher Becomes PM
events.blurb: The leader of the British Conservative Party, a grocer's daughter who had studied chemistry at Oxford and later trained as a barrister, was invited by the monarch to form a government after her party won a sweeping parliamentary majority. She became the United Kingdom's first woman prime minister and would hold the office for 11 years — the longest continuous premiership of the 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1979 — she took office quoting St. Francis of Assisi on the doorstep: "Where there is discord, may we bring harmony." The next decade would be anything but that. She was forced to resign by her own cabinet in November 1990.

events.title: Ruth Bader Ginsburg Confirmed
events.blurb: A 60-year-old federal appeals court judge, a former ACLU lawyer who had successfully argued six of the era's most important gender-discrimination cases before the court she was now joining, was confirmed 96-3 as the second woman to sit on the U.S. Supreme Court. She would serve 27 years, becoming — somewhat unexpectedly for a cautious litigator — a late-life pop-culture icon on the Court's liberal wing.
events.revealBlurb: August 10, 1993 — nominated by Bill Clinton. She acquired the nickname "Notorious RBG" from a law student's Tumblr in 2013. She died September 18, 2020, enabling the confirmation of Amy Coney Barrett eight days before the presidential election.

events.title: Indian Rebellion of 1857
events.blurb: Sepoys of the East India Company's Bengal Army, enraged by rumours that their rifle cartridges had been greased with beef and pork fat, rose in mutiny at a garrison town north of Delhi, shot their British officers, and marched south to proclaim a reluctant Mughal emperor the leader of a broader uprising. The revolt spread across north and central India over the following year.
events.revealBlurb: May 10, 1857 — Meerut. Bahadur Shah Zafar, the 82-year-old titular Mughal, was dragged out of retirement as figurehead. The revolt's brutal suppression ended Company rule in 1858; the British Crown took direct control of India.

events.title: Gandhi Assassinated
events.blurb: A 78-year-old man, walking slowly across a Delhi lawn supported by two of his grandnieces, was shot three times in the chest at point-blank range by a Hindu nationalist who blamed him for indulging Muslims and accepting partition. He fell murmuring the name of a god. He had survived five previous attempts on his life.
events.revealBlurb: January 30, 1948 — the assassin was Nathuram Godse, a former editor of a Hindu nationalist newspaper. He was convicted and executed. Gandhi had warned his secretary that morning that his life's work would not be judged "until after I am dead and gone."

events.title: Tashkent Declaration
events.blurb: After Soviet-mediated talks, the prime ministers of India and Pakistan signed a declaration in a Central Asian Soviet capital to end hostilities and return to the pre-war ceasefire line. The Indian prime minister died of a heart attack in his hotel room the same night, hours after signing. Conspiracy theories about his death have proliferated for decades; no autopsy was performed.
events.revealBlurb: January 10, 1966 — Lal Bahadur Shastri signs, dies in Tashkent. Ayub Khan signed for Pakistan. Indira Gandhi, Nehru's daughter, succeeded Shastri as prime minister within days. Declassified files have never conclusively explained the death.

events.title: Bangladesh Liberation War
events.blurb: Pakistan's army launched a crackdown on the Bengali-speaking eastern wing of its own country, displacing an estimated 10 million refugees across the border into India. India intervened militarily; within thirteen days it had driven the Pakistani army to capitulate in a Bengali capital, where 93,000 surrendered in the largest military surrender since WWII. A new nation was born.
events.revealBlurb: December 3-16, 1971 — victory at the Instrument of Surrender at Ramna Race Course, Dhaka. Bangladesh Liberation Day is December 16. Field Marshal Sam Manekshaw commanded the Indian effort; Lt. General A.A.K. Niazi signed the surrender.

events.title: Narendra Modi Elected PM
events.blurb: A three-term chief minister of a western state led his party to the first single-party majority in an Indian general election in 30 years, campaigning on development, anti-corruption, and Hindu-nationalist themes after ten years of a Congress-led coalition. The ruling party was reduced to 44 seats, its worst defeat since independence. The new prime minister was sworn in at a ceremony attended by leaders from across South Asia.
events.revealBlurb: May 16, 2014 — results declared; Modi sworn in May 26. The BJP won 282 of 543 seats. Modi had been denied a U.S. visa for years over the 2002 Gujarat riots; that travel ban was lifted on his election.

events.title: Kalidas Released — First Tamil Talkie
events.blurb: A mythological musical about the Sanskrit poet Kalidasa opened at Kinema Central in Madras on Diwali and became simultaneously the first sound film in Tamil and the first in Telugu — the hero singing in Telugu, the heroine speaking Tamil, a third actor delivering dialogue in Hindi, making it a multilingual sound experiment disguised as a devotional drama.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1931 — directed by H.M. Reddy, just months after Alam Ara introduced sound to India. A young actor billed only as L.V. Prasad played a cameo; he would later become one of South India's most powerful film producers. The film is now preserved at the National Film Archive.

events.title: Bombay Talkies Founded
events.blurb: A studio established in Malad, Bombay, by a London-trained filmmaker and his aristocratic actress-wife drew European technical talent — German cameramen, British equipment — to build India's first modern film facility with synchronised sound stages and a Western-style star system. It launched the careers of Dilip Kumar, Ashok Kumar, and Madhubala within its first fifteen years.
events.revealBlurb: April 15, 1934 — founded by Himanshu Rai and Devika Rani. Rai died in 1940 while the studio was mid-production; Devika Rani, then 32, took sole control and ran it for another nine years. The studio was where a young Dilip Kumar walked in looking for work and was handed a contract he barely understood.

events.title: Zanjeer Released
events.blurb: After fifteen consecutive flops, a young actor was offered the role of an angry, incorruptible police inspector in a crime thriller that every major star of the decade — Dharmendra, Dev Anand, Rajesh Khanna — had turned down. The film's success redirected an entire industry's idea of what a Hindi film hero could look like: not romantic or comic, but furious.
events.revealBlurb: May 11, 1973 — written by Salim-Javed, directed by Prakash Mehra. Amitabh Bachchan was cast almost by elimination. Salim Khan and Javed Akhtar then wrote nearly every subsequent Bachchan blockbuster with him specifically in mind, insisting on his casting as a contractual condition.

events.title: Deewaar Released
events.blurb: A story of two brothers who grow up in identical poverty but choose radically different paths — one becomes a dock smuggler, the other a policeman — gave Indian cinema one of its defining confrontation scenes. Its dialogue was so tightly constructed that screenwriters Salim-Javed became as famous as directors, the first time a writing duo achieved superstar status in Bollywood.
events.revealBlurb: January 24, 1975 — directed by Yash Chopra. Amitabh Bachchan's character has "mere paas maa hai" spoken against him, not by him — the misattribution became India's most-repeated film misquote. Director's first choices were Dev Anand and Rajesh Khanna; both were unavailable.

events.title: Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge Released
events.blurb: A romance about two Non-Resident Indians falling in love on a Eurorail trip before battling parental disapproval opened in Bombay that autumn and never fully left: it ran continuously at one Mumbai cinema for over two decades, setting a record no Indian film has matched. Its climactic train-platform scene became shorthand for every subsequent Bollywood love story.
events.revealBlurb: October 20, 1995 — Aditya Chopra's directorial debut, age 23. He refused to watch the film with an audience for years. Shah Rukh Khan initially had reservations about the role. The film ran at Mumbai's Maratha Mandir theatre without interruption until 2023 — 1,278 weeks.

events.title: Plessy v. Ferguson
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 7-1 that a Louisiana law requiring "equal but separate" railroad cars for white and Black passengers did not violate the Constitution. The decision invented the "separate but equal" doctrine that underpinned legal segregation for 58 years. Justice John Marshall Harlan's lone dissent declared the Constitution "color-blind" — a minority view for half a century.
events.revealBlurb: May 18, 1896. The plaintiff, Homer Plessy, was 7/8 white; he deliberately boarded a whites-only car to test the law. Harlan, a former slaveholder from Kentucky, wrote the dissent the movement would eventually vindicate.

events.title: Tulsa Race Massacre
events.blurb: An armed white mob, deputized by local police and in some cases flown in biplanes to drop makeshift bombs, attacked an affluent Black neighborhood in an Oklahoma oil city nicknamed "Black Wall Street." Over 18 hours they burned 35 blocks of homes and businesses, killed an estimated 100 to 300 residents, and arrested 6,000 survivors. Nobody was ever prosecuted.
events.revealBlurb: May 31 to June 1, 1921 — Greenwood District, Tulsa. The massacre was scrubbed from local newspapers and school curricula for 75 years. A state commission finally investigated in 2001. Mass graves are still being exhumed.

events.title: Executive Order 8802
events.blurb: Facing a threatened mass march on Washington organized by a prominent Black labor leader, a U.S. president signed an executive order banning racial discrimination in the defense industry and federal government. It was the first federal action against employment discrimination since Reconstruction. The threatened march was called off; the larger March would come 22 years later.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 1941 — Franklin Roosevelt, pushed by A. Philip Randolph. Randolph had assembled 100,000 marchers and refused to call it off without the order. The order created the Fair Employment Practice Committee — a template for later civil rights enforcement.

events.title: Brown v. Board of Education
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court unanimously ruled that racially segregated public schools are "inherently unequal" and therefore unconstitutional, overturning the 58-year-old "separate but equal" doctrine. The narrow ruling on schools would expand over the next decade to strike down segregation in parks, beaches, swimming pools, and every other public facility.
events.revealBlurb: May 17, 1954 — Chief Justice Earl Warren assembled a 9-0 majority despite internal resistance. Enforcement took years; Arkansas governors called out the national guard to bar Black students, and some counties closed their schools entirely rather than integrate.

events.title: Emmett Till Murdered
events.blurb: A 14-year-old Black boy visiting family in a rural Southern state was abducted from his great-uncle's home in the middle of the night, tortured, shot, and thrown into a river with a cotton-gin fan tied around his neck. His mother insisted on an open-casket funeral so the world could see what had been done to her son. Photographs of the mutilated body, published in Jet magazine, galvanized a generation.
events.revealBlurb: August 28, 1955 — Money, Mississippi. His accuser, Carolyn Bryant, admitted decades later she had lied about the encounter. Her husband and his half-brother were acquitted by an all-white jury, then sold their confession to Look magazine knowing they couldn't be retried.

events.title: Scuttling of the Graf Spee
events.blurb: A feared commerce-raider that had sunk nine merchant ships in three months limped into a neutral harbour for repairs after a running battle with three smaller cruisers, then sat immobile while international diplomacy set a 72-hour countdown. Twenty thousand spectators lined the waterfront to watch her captain make his final decision.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1939, Montevideo. Captain Hans Langsdorff scuttled the Admiral Graf Spee at 8:55 PM rather than risk his crew in what he believed was an overwhelming British trap. Three days later he wrapped himself in the ship's battle ensign and shot himself. The trap was largely bluff.

events.title: Battle of Crete
events.blurb: For the first time in military history, an entire island was invaded and captured primarily by paratroopers and glider-borne troops alone, dropped onto an enemy-held coastline in the face of fierce resistance. The attackers suffered such catastrophic losses on the opening day that the tactic was never repeated at this scale.
events.revealBlurb: May 20 – June 1, 1941 — Operation Mercury. German paratroopers suffered over 6,500 casualties, including roughly 3,000 killed. Hitler was so shaken he banned future mass airborne operations. The British, Australian, and New Zealand defenders were evacuated; 5,000 were left behind and taken prisoner.

events.title: Allied Invasion of Sicily
events.blurb: The largest amphibious operation to that point in military history put 160,000 troops, 3,000 ships, and 4,000 aircraft onto a Mediterranean island in a single night and day — opening the Allied campaign on the European continent itself and within three weeks causing the arrest and removal of a dictator who had held power for two decades.
events.revealBlurb: July 9–10, 1943 — Operation Husky. Benito Mussolini was deposed by his own Fascist Grand Council on July 25, just two weeks after the landings. An elaborate Allied deception operation, "Operation Mincemeat," had planted false documents on a corpse washed ashore in Spain suggesting the real target was Greece — and the Germans believed it.

events.title: Fall of Berlin
events.blurb: Soviet forces crossed into a capital city from three sides in a three-week assault involving two million soldiers, fighting block by block through a rubble-strewn metropolis defended by exhausted Wehrmacht troops, elderly home-guard units, and teenagers, while the city's absolute ruler retreated into an underground bunker and refused to concede that the war was lost.
events.revealBlurb: April 16 – May 2, 1945. Stalin had secretly put two Soviet army groups into a race for the Reichstag — willing to accept the extra casualties to ensure the symbolic prize fell to one particular commander. The famous "Victory Banner" was raised at 2:25 PM on April 30. German General Helmuth Weidling surrendered the city garrison on May 2 with fewer than 35,000 malnourished defenders left.

events.title: Victory in Europe Day
events.blurb: Unconditional surrender documents were signed at an Allied headquarters on two successive nights in two different cities, and the moment the ceasefire took effect at one minute past eleven, millions of people in cities across a battered continent poured into the streets to celebrate the end of a conflict that had killed an estimated 70 to 85 million human beings.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1945. Germany signed the first surrender at Reims on May 7; a second signing in Berlin satisfied Soviet demands. Stalin proclaimed May 9 as Victory Day — still observed in Russia today. More than a million people celebrated in the streets across the UK. Churchill told the crowds from a Whitehall balcony: "God bless you all. This is your victory."

events.title: Jamestown Colony Founded
events.blurb: English settlers dispatched by the Virginia Company came ashore on a low, marshy peninsula in the tidewater and drove stakes for the first permanent English settlement in the territory that would become the United States. Of the roughly 104 men and boys who arrived, fewer than 40 survived their first year, undone by brackish drinking water, starvation, and disease.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1607 — Virginia. The site was chosen partly because its deep water let ships dock without anchors — and partly because it looked easy to defend. It was also mosquito-ridden and had no fresh water. Within nine months, roughly 65% of the colonists were dead.

events.title: British Parliament Passes the Stamp Act
events.blurb: Parliament enacted a sweeping tax requiring colonists to purchase revenue stamps for newspapers, legal documents, almanacs, and even playing cards — the first direct tax Britain had ever levied on its American colonies. Outcry was immediate and visceral: colonial assemblies passed resolutions of protest, merchants organized boycotts, and a new network of radicals calling themselves the Sons of Liberty took to the streets.
events.revealBlurb: March 22, 1765 — London. The tax was repealed the following year under merchant pressure, but Parliament simultaneously passed the Declaratory Act asserting its absolute right to tax the colonies "in all cases whatsoever." The colonists celebrated the repeal and mostly ignored the Declaratory Act — for about a decade.

events.title: Monroe Doctrine Declared
events.blurb: An American president's annual address to Congress warned European powers against further colonization or political interference in the Western Hemisphere, a policy the United States could not yet militarily enforce but would cite for the next two centuries. The message was drafted largely by his Secretary of State, a future president himself.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1823 — James Monroe. The phrase "Monroe Doctrine" wasn't coined until 1850. Britain quietly backed the policy because it suited their own trade interests, and for decades the Royal Navy did most of the actual enforcing.

events.title: Atomic Bomb Dropped on Hiroshima
events.blurb: At 8:15 that morning, a B-29 Superfortress named the Enola Gay released a uranium bomb nicknamed "Little Boy" over the Japanese city of Hiroshima, which detonated at 1,968 feet above the city center with a force equivalent to approximately 15,000 tons of TNT. Estimates of deaths in the four months following the explosion range from 90,000 to 166,000; roughly two-thirds of the city's buildings were destroyed.
events.revealBlurb: August 6, 1945 — Hiroshima, Japan. "Little Boy" was the first nuclear weapon ever used in warfare, but it had never been fully tested — scientists were confident enough in the gun-type design. Japan did not surrender after Hiroshima; it took a second bomb (Nagasaki, August 9) to produce the surrender announcement.

events.title: Brown v. Board of Education Ruling
events.blurb: A unanimous Supreme Court held that racially segregated public schools were inherently unequal and violated the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause, overturning the 1896 Plessy v. Ferguson doctrine of "separate but equal." The unanimous 9–0 decision, written by Chief Justice Earl Warren after months of behind-the-scenes persuasion, applied to all public schools and laid the legal foundation for desegregation across American society.
events.revealBlurb: May 17, 1954 — Washington, D.C. Chief Justice Warren had been appointed by Eisenhower, who privately thought the ruling a mistake. The lead attorney for the plaintiffs was Thurgood Marshall — who would later become the first Black justice on the very court he argued before.

events.title: Justinian's Code Issued
events.blurb: A Byzantine emperor's commission of ten jurists, working for 14 months, compiled nearly a thousand years of Roman legal rulings into a single four-part code. It became the foundation of civil-law systems across continental Europe and, centuries later, Latin America. Imperial-era laws contradicted themselves; the code resolved the contradictions by fiat.
events.revealBlurb: April 7, 529 — Emperor Justinian I issued the first edition. The final compilation, called the Corpus Juris Civilis, influenced the Napoleonic Code and every legal system modeled on it. Law students still read excerpts today.

events.title: The Hijra
events.blurb: Fleeing plots against his life in the Arabian trading city where he had preached for 13 years, a 53-year-old prophet and roughly seventy of his followers slipped out at night and rode 320 kilometres north to a rival oasis town whose feuding tribes had invited him to mediate. He arrived to a welcoming reception and began building the first Islamic community under his political authority.
events.revealBlurb: July 16, 622 — Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina. The Islamic calendar begins from this year, not his birth. "Hijra" literally means "emigration" or "severing of ties."

events.title: Genghis Khan Unites the Mongols
events.blurb: A 44-year-old tribal chieftain named Temüjin, having spent two decades defeating his rivals across the eastern steppe, was acclaimed "Universal Ruler" at an assembly of chieftains beside a sacred river. Within two decades his cavalry armies would sack Beijing, overrun Persia, and reach the Adriatic, creating the largest contiguous land empire in history.
events.revealBlurb: 1206 — at the Onon River. The title "Genghis Khan" is a western rendering; contemporary Mongol sources call him Činggis Qa'an. Genetic studies suggest roughly 16 million men alive today descend from his Y-chromosome line.

events.title: Marco Polo Departs for China
events.blurb: A 17-year-old Venetian merchant's son set out with his father and uncle on a journey across Asia to the court of the Mongol emperor. He would return to Venice 24 years later and, captured in a war with Genoa three years after that, dictate an account of his travels to a cellmate. The resulting book became the most influential western description of Asia for the next three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: 1271 — Marco left Venice with Niccolò and Maffeo Polo. Returning in 1295, he was imprisoned by the Genoese; his cellmate Rustichello da Pisa helped him write "Il Milione." Christopher Columbus's annotated copy survives.

events.title: Siege of Orléans Lifted
events.blurb: A 17-year-old peasant girl from Lorraine, dressed in white armour and claiming visions from saints, led a French relief army into a besieged Loire Valley city. Over eight days of sorties, she personally led assaults on the English siege forts around the city, was shot through the shoulder with a crossbow bolt, returned to the fight, and broke the siege. The French war effort, exhausted for a generation, was transformed overnight.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1429 — Joan of Arc relieves Orléans. She had convinced a skeptical Dauphin to give her an army by passing a theological interrogation and, reportedly, a virginity test. She would see him crowned as Charles VII at Reims within ten weeks.

events.title: Rubik's Cube Global Craze
events.blurb: A 3×3 mechanical puzzle cube invented six years earlier by a Hungarian architecture professor became a global bestseller after licensed international distribution began. Over 100 million units sold in the first three years. Books of solutions appeared on bestseller lists. The puzzle's simplicity — six colours, 43 quintillion possible states, a single solved configuration — caught people who had never bought a toy in their lives. World championships began in 1982.
events.revealBlurb: 1981 — Ernő Rubik had patented the cube in 1975; it went international in 1980. The first world championship was in Budapest, June 5, 1982; the current world record for solving it is under 3.05 seconds (Max Park, June 2023). The cube remains in continuous production.

events.title: Apple's "1984" Super Bowl Ad
events.blurb: A 60-second commercial produced by a British director for a California computer company aired during the third quarter of the Super Bowl. The ad showed a dystopian audience of grey workers watching a Big-Brother-like speaker on a vast screen; an athletic woman in running clothes smashed the screen with a hammer. The product was the Macintosh computer. Apple's board had voted to kill the ad; the CEO insisted it air. It aired once.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 1984 — directed by Ridley Scott. The ad ran nationally only that one time; it has since been shown as a promotion or film-clip thousands of times. Macintosh sales in its first 100 days exceeded expectations. The "1984" ad is still considered one of the greatest commercials ever made.

events.title: Top Gun Released
events.blurb: A 91-minute naval aviation film starring a 23-year-old actor as an arrogant fighter pilot attending an elite Navy flight-training school became the highest-grossing film of the year. The Pentagon had collaborated on the production, providing F-14 Tomcats, aircraft carriers, and expert technical advice in exchange for script approval and recruitment-friendly portrayals. Navy recruiting offices saw a 500 percent jump in inquiries. The soundtrack, led by "Danger Zone," hit number one.
events.revealBlurb: May 16, 1986 — Tony Scott directing Tom Cruise. Recruiting offices were set up in theatre lobbies showing the film. A sequel — "Top Gun: Maverick" — finally arrived in 2022 after multiple delays, grossing $1.5 billion worldwide.

events.title: Titanic Released
events.blurb: A Canadian director released a 195-minute romantic epic about a fictional couple aboard the 1912 maiden voyage of the British ocean liner. The production had been the most expensive in Hollywood history, its budget having doubled during filming; industry wags predicted financial disaster. The film ran in theatres for ten months, won 11 Oscars, and became the first film to gross over a billion dollars. Its director famously shouted "I'm king of the world" from the podium.
events.revealBlurb: December 19, 1997 — James Cameron, starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Kate Winslet. It grossed $2.2 billion; Cameron's subsequent "Avatar" beat it 12 years later, also directed by him. Celine Dion's "My Heart Will Go On" spent three weeks at #1.

events.title: Furby Released
events.blurb: A battery-operated toy furry pet that could speak, move its eyes, and apparently learn English words from "Furbish" over time became the must-have Christmas gift of the season. Parents who had lived through the Cabbage Patch Kids and Tickle Me Elmo crazes of previous years went through it again. The National Security Agency banned them from their premises, reportedly out of concern that they might record classified conversations and "repeat" them.
events.revealBlurb: October 2, 1998 — Tiger Electronics. 40 million Furbys sold in the first three years. The NSA's ban was based on a misunderstanding of the toy's technology — it had no recording capability at all; "learning" was a pre-programmed script that made the toy seem to become more English-speaking over time.

events.title: Boston Tea Party
events.blurb: That winter night, some 116 colonists disguised as Mohawk warriors boarded three ships in Boston Harbor and dumped 342 chests of East India Company tea into the water, destroying approximately £10,000 worth of merchandise. The targeted destruction was a direct protest against the Tea Act, which granted the company a monopoly while taxing colonial consumers.
events.revealBlurb: December 16, 1773 — Boston Harbor. Not a single participant was ever prosecuted. Britain's furious response — the Coercive Acts, which colonists renamed the Intolerable Acts — did more to unify colonial resistance than the tea party itself. The name "Boston Tea Party" wasn't coined until decades later.

events.title: Battles of Lexington and Concord
events.blurb: That spring morning, British regulars marching to seize a colonial weapons cache at Concord, Massachusetts, exchanged fire with local militia at Lexington before the colonists scattered; at Concord's North Bridge, a second volley triggered a running battle that chased the redcoats back to Boston. The day produced roughly 300 total casualties and the phrase "the shot heard round the world."
events.revealBlurb: April 19, 1775 — Lexington and Concord, Massachusetts. Nobody knows who fired first at Lexington — colonial accounts and British accounts flatly contradict each other. The phrase "shot heard round the world" was written by Ralph Waldo Emerson in 1837, over 60 years after the fact.

events.title: Caning of Senator Charles Sumner
events.blurb: Representative Preston Brooks of South Carolina strode onto the Senate floor and beat Senator Charles Sumner of Massachusetts unconscious with a metal-topped gutta-percha cane, inflicting such severe head injuries that Sumner could not return to his seat for over three years. The assault came two days after Sumner delivered a blistering antislavery speech mocking Brooks's cousin; Massachusetts left Sumner's empty desk on display as a rebuke.
events.revealBlurb: May 22, 1856 — U.S. Senate chamber. Brooks resigned, was immediately re-elected by South Carolina, and received commemorative canes inscribed "Hit Him Again." Sumner's empty desk served as visible propaganda for the antislavery cause for three years. The incident convinced many Northerners that slavery corrupted men beyond reason.

events.title: Pullman Strike and Federal Injunction
events.blurb: When the Pullman Company cut wages by 25 percent without reducing rents in its company-owned town south of Chicago, nearly 4,000 workers walked out that spring; within weeks, the American Railway Union's boycott of Pullman cars had paralyzed rail traffic across 29 railroads and 27 states. President Grover Cleveland dispatched federal troops and obtained a court injunction to break the strike, establishing the federal government's willingness to use military force against organized labor.
events.revealBlurb: May 11, 1894 — Pullman, Illinois. Eugene Debs, the ARU leader, served six months in federal prison for defying the injunction — and read socialist literature in his cell, emerging as America's most famous socialist. The strike also created Labor Day as a federal holiday, rushed through Congress as a conciliation gesture two days before Debs was arrested.

events.title: Black Sunday: The Dust Bowl's Worst Storm
events.blurb: That spring Sunday, a wall of dust estimated at 500 to 600 feet high swept across the southern Great Plains at 60 miles per hour, blotting out the sun and turning a warm afternoon into absolute darkness across Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, and Colorado. The storm — the worst of dozens of black blizzards that had devastated the region since 1930 — was the event that gave the entire catastrophe its name: reporter Robert Geiger called the region "the Dust Bowl" the next day.
events.revealBlurb: April 14, 1935 — Southern Great Plains. An estimated 300,000 tons of topsoil were displaced in a single afternoon. The Dust Bowl ultimately displaced approximately 3.5 million people from the Great Plains — the largest internal migration in American history to that point.

events.title: Shrek Released
events.blurb: A computer-animated feature film from a newly spun-off American studio opened with a green ogre's retelling of classic fairy tales — sly, irreverent, and saturated with pop-culture references aimed at adults as much as children. The film grossed $484 million on an $60 million budget, won the first-ever Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, and made the singing-talking-donkey a cultural touchstone. It would spawn three sequels and establish DreamWorks Animation as a serious rival to Pixar.
events.revealBlurb: May 18, 2001 — DreamWorks Animation. Directors Andrew Adamson and Vicky Jenson; voice cast Mike Myers, Eddie Murphy, Cameron Diaz. The original voice for Shrek was Chris Farley, who died in 1997; the role was recast and rewritten for Myers.

events.title: YouTube Launched
events.blurb: Three former PayPal employees, reportedly frustrated that they couldn't easily share a video of a dinner party or (by an alternate legend) a wardrobe malfunction from a recent sporting event, registered a domain name for a video-sharing site. The site's first uploaded video, "Me at the zoo," was an 18-second clip of one of the founders standing in front of elephants at the San Diego Zoo. Google bought them for $1.65 billion in stock twenty months later.
events.revealBlurb: February 14, 2005 — Chad Hurley, Steve Chen, Jawed Karim. The "Me at the zoo" video is still online, with over 350 million views. Users now upload over 500 hours of video every minute.

events.title: Balloon Boy Hoax
events.blurb: A Colorado family reported that their 6-year-old son had been carried aloft in a homemade silver mylar weather balloon that had drifted off from their backyard. National news networks covered the balloon's two-hour, 80-kilometre flight live, interrupting regular programming. The balloon landed empty. The boy was found hiding in the family attic. Within a day, the father admitted the whole thing had been a publicity stunt, hoping to land the family a reality-TV show.
events.revealBlurb: October 15, 2009 — Heene family, Fort Collins, CO. The father Richard Heene was convicted of a felony and served 30 days; the mother Mayumi got misdemeanor charges. The Heenes reportedly received a pardon from Colorado governor Jared Polis in December 2020.

events.title: Lady Gaga's Meat Dress
events.blurb: A 24-year-old American pop singer arrived at a New York awards show wearing an outfit made from 50 pounds of raw Argentine beef — flank steak fashioned into a sleeveless dress, a matching hat, a handbag, and shoes. She told a late-night host the ensemble was a protest against a military policy excluding openly gay service members. PETA criticized it; steak prices nationwide did not apparently change. The dress was later preserved as beef jerky and displayed at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame.
events.revealBlurb: September 12, 2010 — Lady Gaga (Stefani Germanotta) at the MTV VMAs. Designer Franc Fernandez. The dress won her five VMAs that night, including Video of the Year for "Bad Romance." It is now permanently on display in Cleveland.

events.title: Game of Thrones Finale
events.blurb: The final episode of an HBO fantasy series that had run eight seasons, adapting a popular unfinished novel sequence, drew 19.3 million viewers — the largest audience ever for the show. Viewer reaction to the final season's plot choices was among the most negative ever recorded for a major TV finale; 1.8 million fans signed a petition asking for a reshoot. The series had been, at its peak, the world's single most-pirated television program and a cultural obsession on multiple continents.
events.revealBlurb: May 19, 2019 — series finale, "The Iron Throne." Showrunners David Benioff and D.B. Weiss. The source novels by George R.R. Martin remained unfinished in 2024. HBO went on to produce a prequel series, "House of the Dragon" (2022-), which won back much of the audience.

events.title: Standard of Ur
events.blurb: Craftsmen in a wealthy Sumerian city-state inlaid a hollow wooden box the size of a laptop with lapis lazuli, red limestone, and shell to depict scenes of war on one side and peace on the other, reading top to bottom like a graphic novel. It was buried in a royal tomb and rediscovered only in 1927. Its original function is still debated — a musical instrument's soundbox, perhaps, or a processional standard.
events.revealBlurb: c. 2600 BCE — excavated by Leonard Woolley at the Royal Cemetery of Ur in modern Iraq. Now in the British Museum. Each inlaid figure is made of hundreds of pieces no larger than a fingernail.

events.title: Bayeux Tapestry Completed
events.blurb: An embroidered strip of linen 70 metres long and 50 centimetres high, worked in coloured wool yarns, depicts in 58 scenes the Norman conquest of a cross-Channel kingdom — the diplomatic prelude, the invasion fleet, a victorious battle, and the death of a king by arrow. It includes 623 human figures, 202 horses, 55 dogs, and a Latin commentary running across the top.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1077 — commissioned either by Bishop Odo of Bayeux or Queen Matilda. Despite its name, it is technically embroidery, not tapestry. It survived the French Revolution only because a local lawyer hid it when a crowd tried to use it to cover an ammunition wagon.

events.title: Dürer's Self-Portrait
events.blurb: A 28-year-old German painter and printmaker completed a small panel depicting himself facing the viewer head-on, with long centre-parted hair and his right hand raised in a gesture traditionally reserved for depictions of Christ. It was a provocative piece of self-fashioning — the artist as holy creator. The inscription beside his head, dated to the year, pointed out how few European painters had ever signed their own faces.
events.revealBlurb: 1500 — Albrecht Dürer. Now in Munich's Alte Pinakothek. Dürer's German contemporaries thought the pose bordered on blasphemous. The picture has been read as the first true self-portrait-as-self-expression in Western art.

events.title: Michelangelo's David Unveiled
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Florentine sculptor unveiled a 5.17-metre marble nude of a biblical hero, carved over three years from a single block of Carrara marble that had been rejected by two earlier sculptors as flawed. The statue was intended for the rooftop of a cathedral; a committee that included Leonardo da Vinci decided the work was too significant to put out of sight and instead installed it in the main square of the city.
events.revealBlurb: September 8, 1504 — Michelangelo Buonarroti. Moving it from the workshop to the Piazza della Signoria took 40 men 4 days. The statue was damaged by a mob in 1527 and by a 1991 attack with a hammer; it now stands indoors at the Accademia, where a copy watches over the piazza.

events.title: Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring
events.blurb: A Dutch painter in his early thirties completed an intimate oil study on canvas of a young woman turning toward the viewer, her head covered in a blue and yellow turban, a single teardrop-shaped pearl catching the light at her ear. It was not a commissioned portrait but a "tronie" — a character study. The artist made only about 35 paintings in his career; this one was rediscovered in 1881 at auction for two guilders.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1665 — Johannes Vermeer. Now in the Mauritshuis in The Hague. The "pearl" may actually be tin or glass — no pearl of that size is plausible. Tracy Chevalier's 1999 novel and the 2003 film made it a pop-culture icon.

events.title: Vesalius Publishes De Fabrica
events.blurb: A 28-year-old Flemish anatomist at the University of Padua published a lavishly illustrated seven-volume atlas of human anatomy based on dissections he had performed personally, often on the bodies of recently executed criminals. Many of the 273 woodcut illustrations contradicted established Galenic teachings on points ranging from the structure of the jawbone to the absence of a hole between the heart's chambers. The book launched anatomy as a modern evidence-based science.
events.revealBlurb: 1543 — Andreas Vesalius, "De Humani Corporis Fabrica." The illustrations were probably drawn by students of Titian. Vesalius' enemies in traditional medical faculties fought him bitterly; he burned his own unpublished work in despair at one point and entered court life, dying on a pilgrimage 21 years later.

events.title: Jenner's First Vaccination
events.blurb: A 47-year-old English country doctor in Gloucestershire inoculated an 8-year-old boy with pus scraped from the hand of a milkmaid who had contracted cowpox, a mild disease related to smallpox but harmless in humans. Six weeks later he inoculated the boy with actual smallpox. The boy did not get sick. The doctor wrote up his results, which transformed public health across the world over the next two centuries.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1796 — Edward Jenner inoculated James Phipps. The word "vaccine" comes from vacca (Latin for cow). Jenner refused to patent the procedure despite the enormous potential fortune, insisting it was a gift to humanity. Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 — the only disease eliminated through vaccination.

events.title: First Ether Anesthesia Demo
events.blurb: A Boston dentist administered inhaled diethyl ether vapour to a patient in the surgical amphitheatre of Massachusetts General Hospital, rendering him unconscious while a leading surgeon removed a tumour from his neck. The patient woke pain-free. The surgeon turned to the assembled observers and said, "Gentlemen, this is no humbug." Surgical anesthesia had arrived; the previous era of surgery as fast, agonizing amputations in the patient's full consciousness was ending.
events.revealBlurb: October 16, 1846 — dentist William T. G. Morton and surgeon John Collins Warren at MGH, Boston. The amphitheatre, now called the "Ether Dome," is preserved as a National Historic Landmark. Morton spent the rest of his life in failed litigation trying to collect royalties on the technique.

events.title: Fleming Discovers Penicillin
events.blurb: A 47-year-old Scottish bacteriologist returning from a summer holiday to his London laboratory noticed that one of the staphylococcus-culture plates he had left stacked on his bench had been contaminated by a mold, and that a clear zone of inhibition around the mold showed the bacteria had died there. He identified the mold genus, isolated an anti-bacterial substance it produced, and published his findings — which were largely ignored for over a decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 28, 1928 — Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital, London. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford successfully purified penicillin in 1941, making it a usable drug. They shared the 1945 Nobel with Fleming. The drug's mass production during WWII saved hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers' lives.

events.title: HIV Identified
events.blurb: A research team at a Paris institute published a paper in the journal Science describing a new retrovirus, isolated from a lymph node of a patient with lymphadenopathy, which they believed to be the cause of AIDS. A parallel American team would publish a similar finding a year later; the credit dispute between the labs lasted years and contributed to delayed public health responses. The virus had probably crossed into humans from chimpanzees in central Africa in the early 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: May 20, 1983 — Françoise Barré-Sinoussi, Luc Montagnier at Institut Pasteur. Robert Gallo at the US National Cancer Institute made a similar claim in 1984. The French were eventually credited as discoverers and won the 2008 Nobel. 40 million people have died of AIDS; antiretroviral therapy since 1996 has made it a manageable chronic disease.

events.title: Plato's Republic
events.blurb: An Athenian philosopher completed a ten-book Socratic dialogue in which his deceased teacher argues with several interlocutors about the nature of justice and, by extension, the ideal city. The work would become the foundational text of Western political philosophy; its allegory of the cave, its philosopher-king proposal, and its ban on poets have been quoted, contested, and imitated ever since.
events.revealBlurb: c. 380 BCE — Plato. Alfred North Whitehead famously called European philosophy "a series of footnotes to Plato." The Republic was unknown in the medieval Latin West until the Renaissance; it reached Islamic and Byzantine scholars first.

events.title: Chaucer's Canterbury Tales
events.blurb: An English civil servant in his mid-fifties died leaving unfinished a collection of stories told by pilgrims riding from Southwark to a Kentish cathedral shrine. Written in Middle English rather than French or Latin, the work demonstrated the poetic range of the English vernacular across a social spectrum — knights, millers, cooks, pardoners, the famously bawdy Wife of Bath. Only 24 of a planned 120 tales were ever completed.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1400 — Geoffrey Chaucer. He is often called the father of English literature. Roughly 80 manuscripts survive; the earliest complete ones date from the 1410s. The Wife of Bath's Tale became an early feminist touchstone.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Printed
events.blurb: A goldsmith in a Rhine-valley city completed the first book printed in Europe using movable metal type — a Latin Bible set in 42 lines per page, bound in 180 copies. His press combined existing technologies — oil-based ink, a wine-press frame, cast-metal punches — into an invention that would be blamed for everything from the Reformation to the Renaissance to modern literacy.
events.revealBlurb: 1455 — Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz. Forty-nine copies are known to survive; roughly twenty are complete. Gutenberg himself was sued by his financier the same year and lost the press.

events.title: Treasure Island Published
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Scottish writer, suffering severe pulmonary illness and convalescing in the Scottish Highlands, sketched a treasure map with his 12-year-old stepson on a rainy afternoon and began improvising a story for the boy. The serialized pirate adventure novel that grew from the map — featuring a peg-legged cook, a squawking parrot, a buried fortune, and a black spot — essentially defined the iconography of piracy for the next century and a half.
events.revealBlurb: November 14, 1883 — Robert Louis Stevenson. Initially serialized in the magazine Young Folks in 1881 as "The Sea Cook." The phrase "Shiver me timbers!" does not appear in the book but was popularized by its Long John Silver.

events.title: Dracula Published
events.blurb: A 49-year-old Irish theatrical manager, who had spent seven years researching Eastern European folklore, vampire legends, and a medieval Romanian voivode in his spare time while running a London theatre for the period's most famous actor, published an epistolary horror novel constructed from letters, diary entries, and newspaper clippings. The book was reviewed respectably but sold modestly. Its true career began with stage and film adaptations in subsequent decades.
events.revealBlurb: May 26, 1897 — Bram Stoker. The historical figure he borrowed the name from, Vlad III Dracula (Vlad the Impaler), was a Wallachian prince with no known vampiric habits. F. W. Murnau's unauthorized 1922 silent film Nosferatu nearly led the Stoker estate to destroy every print.

events.title: Turing's Computable Numbers
events.blurb: A 23-year-old British mathematician submitted a paper describing a hypothetical abstract machine — an infinite tape with a movable read/write head obeying a simple finite rule table — that could in principle compute anything a human mathematician could work out by following a procedure. The paper was intended to settle a famous open problem in formal logic; along the way it laid the mathematical groundwork for general-purpose computing.
events.revealBlurb: 1936 — Alan Turing, "On Computable Numbers." Written while he was a 23-year-old student. Turing worked with a physical analogue of the machine at Bletchley Park during WWII to break German Enigma ciphers. He was chemically castrated for homosexuality and died in 1954, probably by suicide.

events.title: First Cellular Phone Call
events.blurb: A Motorola engineer, standing on a Manhattan street with a 1.1-kilogram "brick" prototype handset to his ear, placed a phone call to his chief rival at a competing company's research lab — and made sure to inform him what he was doing. The handset's battery gave 35 minutes of talk time after 10 hours of charging. Motorola would spend another decade getting a lighter version to market.
events.revealBlurb: April 3, 1973 — Martin Cooper of Motorola called Joel Engel at Bell Labs. The prototype was the DynaTAC 8000x. It sold commercially in 1983 for $3,995. Cooper later said he'd been inspired by the communicator in Star Trek.

events.title: Ethernet Invented
events.blurb: An engineer at a Palo Alto research lab, inspired partly by a Hawaiian university's packet-radio network, drafted a memo describing a coaxial-cable local-area network that let multiple computers share a single transmission medium by listening before sending and backing off when collisions occurred. The protocol became the physical backbone of essentially every wired office and data-center network in the world.
events.revealBlurb: May 22, 1973 — Bob Metcalfe at Xerox PARC. He later co-founded 3Com to sell Ethernet products and became one of Silicon Valley's most quotable pundits. Metcalfe's Law — that a network's value grows with the square of its users — is named for him.

events.title: Apple Computer Founded
events.blurb: Two 20-something Californians, a college dropout and a self-taught engineer, formed a partnership to sell a printed-circuit-board computer design the engineer had developed and the dropout had realized was marketable. A third partner, older and more cautious, asked out within two weeks and sold his share back for $800. The initial product was a hand-built board requiring the buyer to supply their own power supply, keyboard, and case.
events.revealBlurb: April 1, 1976 — Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne. Wayne's 10 percent share would today be worth over $300 billion. He has said he doesn't regret selling out; he'd been in a startup before and wanted to avoid another personal-liability exposure.

events.title: IBM PC Released
events.blurb: The world's dominant mainframe computer maker released a small desktop machine built, unusually for the company, from off-the-shelf parts — an Intel 8088 processor, an operating system licensed from Microsoft, components any competitor could buy. Business customers trusted the name and bought millions. The design's open specifications led to a decade of "IBM compatible" clones that collectively made the Intel/Microsoft duopoly inevitable.
events.revealBlurb: August 12, 1981 — IBM PC model 5150. It had 16KB of RAM and no hard drive. IBM's decision to source DOS from Microsoft, rather than write it in-house, is usually cited as the great strategic error of 20th-century computing. Gates retained all distribution rights.

events.title: Columbus Reaches the Americas
