events.blurb: A Genoese navigator captaining three small Spanish ships, after 33 days of open-Atlantic sailing from the Canary Islands with an increasingly mutinous crew, sighted land just after 2 AM — a low-lying island he promptly named after a Christian saviour. He was convinced, and would die still convinced, that he had reached the outer islands of Asia. The four voyages he made over the next twelve years reshaped two continents.
events.revealBlurb: October 12, 1492 — Christopher Columbus made landfall on Guanahani in the Bahamas. The lookout who first sighted land, Rodrigo de Triana, did not receive the promised reward — Columbus claimed he had seen a light the previous evening. The contact collapsed Indigenous populations via epidemic disease within decades.

events.title: Copernicus's De Revolutionibus
events.blurb: A 70-year-old Polish mathematician and canon of a cathedral in Warmia died on the same day he was reportedly handed a freshly printed copy of the book he had been writing, revising, and withholding from publication for three decades. The book, On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, argued that the earth was a planet orbiting the sun, and that the apparent daily motion of the heavens was actually the earth's own rotation. It was placed on the Papal Index 73 years later.
events.revealBlurb: May 24, 1543 — Nicolaus Copernicus died. The book's printer, Andreas Osiander, had added an anonymous preface describing its heliocentrism as a mere mathematical convenience; Copernicus probably never saw that preface. Galileo, who openly defended heliocentrism, was tried for heresy in 1633.

events.title: Spanish Armada Defeated
events.blurb: A Spanish naval force of 130 ships and 26,000 men, intended to escort a Flemish invasion army across the Channel to England, was met by a faster, more maneuverable English fleet off the Flanders coast. An English fireship attack scattered the Spanish anchorage overnight; the following day's running battle crippled the armada. Storms in the North Sea and along the Irish coast destroyed the rest on the long retreat home. Barely half returned to Spain.
events.revealBlurb: July 29 to August 8, 1588 — Battle of Gravelines decided it. English commanders: Lord Howard of Effingham, Sir Francis Drake. Roughly 35 Spanish ships reached home; most of the rest were wrecked on the Irish coast, whose people dealt harshly with survivors.

events.title: Galileo's Telescope Observations
events.blurb: A 46-year-old Paduan university mathematics professor, having improved the magnification of a newly invented Dutch optical toy from 3x to 30x, pointed his telescope at the night sky. Over the following months he observed craters on the moon, four previously unknown moons circling Jupiter, phases of Venus, and individual stars resolvable in the milky white band of the Milky Way. His findings, published in a short Latin book, transformed astronomy.
events.revealBlurb: January 7, 1610 — Galileo Galilei observed Jupiter's moons from Padua. His book "Sidereus Nuncius" (The Starry Messenger) was rushed into print in March. The phases of Venus, observed later that year, were decisive evidence against the Ptolemaic earth-centered model.

events.title: Defenestration of Prague
events.blurb: Two Catholic imperial officials and their secretary were thrown from the windows of a castle tower by a Protestant Bohemian noble deputation enraged by Habsburg religious policies. The three men fell 21 metres into a pile of manure and survived; the Catholics said angels had caught them. The incident triggered a Protestant revolt that spread into the Thirty Years War — a continent-wide conflict that would kill eight million people before a 1648 peace.
events.revealBlurb: May 23, 1618 — Prague Castle. The officials were Vilém Slavata and Jaroslav Bořita of Martinice, along with their secretary Filip Fabricius. Fabricius was ennobled by the emperor as "Baron von Hohenfall" — "Baron of the Great Fall."

events.title: First Ancient Olympic Games
events.blurb: A religious festival held every four years in honour of Zeus at a sacred grove in the western Peloponnese began with a single footrace — a sprint of about 192 metres — won by a cook from the nearby city of Elis. Over subsequent centuries, the games expanded to include additional running events, wrestling, boxing, pankration, pentathlon, and chariot racing. The festival ran continuously for nearly 1,200 years before a Christian emperor banned it.
events.revealBlurb: 776 BCE — traditional date of first games at Olympia; winner Coroebus of Elis. The festival was abolished by Emperor Theodosius I in 393 CE as part of his suppression of pagan rites. It was revived as the modern Olympics in Athens, 1896.

events.title: FIFA Founded
events.blurb: Representatives of seven European national football associations — Belgium, Denmark, France, Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland — met at a Paris sports association's offices and established an international governing body for the sport. England, which had invented the modern codified game and considered itself the natural authority, declined to attend, joined in 1905, and withdrew multiple times over subsequent decades in petty disputes. The organization would run the World Cup from 1930 on.
events.revealBlurb: May 21, 1904 — Fédération Internationale de Football Association, Paris. Its first president was Robert Guérin. FIFA now has 211 member associations, more than the UN. Its headquarters moved to Zurich in 1932 and have been there since.

events.title: Hillary and Tenzing Summit Everest
events.blurb: A 33-year-old New Zealand beekeeper and a 39-year-old Nepalese sherpa, the final two-man summit party of a British Himalayan expedition, stepped onto the top of the world's highest mountain at 11:30 AM local time after a four-hour climb from their high camp. They spent fifteen minutes at the top, took photographs, and buried a few mementos in the snow. News reached London on the morning of the queen's coronation four days later.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1953 — Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay, British expedition under John Hunt. They never conclusively settled which of them stepped onto the summit first; both said it didn't matter. The news coincided with Queen Elizabeth II's coronation, making it front-page across the Commonwealth.

events.title: Magic Johnson Announces HIV
events.blurb: A 32-year-old Lakers star held a nationally televised press conference announcing he would be retiring from the NBA immediately, because he had tested positive for HIV. The announcement — at a moment when the virus was widely associated with gay men and intravenous drug users — instantly changed public perception of who could contract AIDS. He had learned the result days earlier during a routine pre-insurance physical. He would unretire briefly twice, including to play an All-Star Game and the 1992 Olympics.
events.revealBlurb: November 7, 1991 — Earvin "Magic" Johnson at the Los Angeles Forum. He remains alive and visibly healthy over 30 years later, thanks to antiretroviral therapy. His announcement drove huge increases in HIV testing, awareness, and research funding. He returned to the NBA for a 32-game 1995-96 comeback.

events.title: Messi Wins World Cup
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Argentine forward, in his fifth and final World Cup tournament, led his team to a 3-3 draw against France in the final, then won a penalty shootout 4-2 at a Qatari stadium. He scored two of the final's goals himself, then converted his penalty. The tournament's signature absence from his glittering career — the World Cup — was at last his. It was widely described as the greatest World Cup final ever played.
events.revealBlurb: December 18, 2022 — Argentina 3-3 France (4-2 pens), Lusail Stadium, Qatar. Messi and Kylian Mbappé combined for six goals between them. Messi had already won seven Ballon d'Or awards, a record; he would win an eighth in 2023. Mbappé became the first to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final since Geoff Hurst in 1966.

events.title: 15th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: A constitutional amendment prohibiting the denial of voting rights "on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude" was ratified, giving Black men the theoretical right to vote. Within three decades, poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses, and organized terror had effectively erased Black voting across the former Confederacy.
events.revealBlurb: February 3, 1870. It took the Voting Rights Act of 1965 — 95 years later — to make the amendment's promise practical. Black women were excluded not by race but by sex until the 19th Amendment in 1920.

events.title: Military Desegregation Order
events.blurb: A U.S. president signed an executive order mandating "equality of treatment and opportunity" in the armed forces without regard to race, color, religion, or national origin. The army resisted for nearly five years; full integration of combat units was not achieved until the Korean War made ignoring Black replacements impossible.
events.revealBlurb: July 26, 1948 — Executive Order 9981, Harry Truman. He signed it partly out of conviction, partly because Black voters in northern cities were now pivotal to Democratic victory. The last all-Black unit was dissolved in 1954.

events.title: Birmingham Children's Crusade
events.blurb: Over several days in a notoriously segregated Alabama steel city, more than a thousand Black schoolchildren — some as young as 6 — marched out of classes in organized protest. Police commissioner Bull Connor ordered fire hoses and attack dogs deployed against them. Photographs of a teenage boy lunged at by a German shepherd appeared on front pages across the world.
events.revealBlurb: May 2-5, 1963 — Birmingham, Alabama. King agreed to use children over the objections of many advisers; they were less vulnerable to losing jobs for protesting. Within weeks, the Kennedy administration introduced what became the Civil Rights Act.

events.title: Stonewall Riots
events.blurb: A routine police raid on a Mafia-owned gay bar in a Greenwich Village of Manhattan turned into a six-night uprising when patrons — many of them drag queens, street kids, and trans people of color — fought back rather than submit to arrest. The confrontation catalyzed the modern LGBTQ rights movement; the first Pride marches were held on its first anniversary.
events.revealBlurb: June 28, 1969 — Stonewall Inn, NYC. Pivotal figures included Marsha P. Johnson and Sylvia Rivera. The riot ignited the Gay Liberation Front, which modeled itself on the Black Panthers. June is now Pride Month across much of the world.

events.title: George Floyd Murdered
events.blurb: A 46-year-old Black man was killed in a Midwestern American city when a white police officer kneeled on his neck for 9 minutes and 29 seconds while he was handcuffed face-down on the pavement. A 17-year-old bystander filmed the entire encounter on her phone. The video triggered the largest protest movement in American history — 15 to 26 million people marched across all 50 states over the following weeks.
events.revealBlurb: May 25, 2020 — Minneapolis, officer Derek Chauvin. The bystander was Darnella Frazier; she received a Pulitzer Prize special citation. Chauvin was convicted of second-degree murder 11 months later and sentenced to 22 years. Protests spread to more than 60 countries.

events.title: Dunkirk Evacuation
events.blurb: Over nine days, 338,000 soldiers trapped against the sea by encircling armoured forces were lifted off a French beach by an improvised armada of naval destroyers, ferries, fishing boats, and private pleasure craft — while a rearguard held a tightening perimeter and aircraft fought overhead to keep the sky contested.
events.revealBlurb: May 26 – June 4, 1940 — Operation Dynamo. Planners hoped to save 45,000 men; they got 338,226. The "little ships" — about 700 civilian vessels ranging from lifeboats to Thames paddle steamers — became a national legend. Churchill warned Parliament not to call it a victory: "Wars are not won by evacuations."

events.title: "We Shall Fight" Speech
events.blurb: A prime minister who had been in office barely a month stood in a parliamentary chamber and delivered a report on a catastrophic military retreat, then pivoted to an uncompromising catalogue of every terrain — beaches, landing grounds, fields, streets, hills — across which his country would resist, closing with a flat refusal to ever surrender.
events.revealBlurb: June 4, 1940 — Churchill's "We Shall Fight on the Beaches" speech to the House of Commons. He reportedly muttered to a colleague immediately after: "And we'll fight them with the butt ends of broken beer bottles because that's bloody well all we've got." The line never made the official record.

events.title: Enigma Broken at Bletchley
events.blurb: A team of mathematicians and linguists working in a cluttered hut in the English countryside deployed an electromechanical machine that could test thousands of rotor settings per minute, cracking the daily-changed cipher used by an opposing military's command and logistics networks — and began reading intercepted messages within hours of their transmission.
events.revealBlurb: May 1940 — Bletchley Park's upgraded Bombe, designed by Alan Turing and Gordon Welchman, began breaking Luftwaffe "Red" traffic daily. The secret was so tightly held that some commanders were fed cover stories about lucky reconnaissance flights. The intelligence was codenamed Ultra and arguably shortened the conflict by two years.

events.title: V-2 Rocket's First Successful Test
events.blurb: A 14-metre liquid-fuelled rocket rose from a Baltic coast test site, climbed above the atmosphere, and travelled 190 kilometres before splashing down — the first object built by human hands to reach space, demonstrating a weapon that could strike cities at supersonic speed with no interception possible by any existing technology.
events.revealBlurb: October 3, 1942, Peenemünde. General Walter Dornberger declared: "This third day of October is the first day of a new era, that of space travel." The same technology later launched the first satellites and moon rockets. The V-2's wartime manufacture killed more people in slave-labour production than it killed as a weapon.

events.title: Warsaw Uprising
events.blurb: A resistance army launched an all-out urban insurrection timed to coincide with an approaching allied army's arrival at the city's eastern bank, intending to liberate the capital before that army entered — but the expected support never came, leaving 40,000 fighters and 200,000 civilians to a 63-day battle against overwhelming force that ended in total destruction.
events.revealBlurb: August 1 – October 2, 1944. The Polish Home Army rose at 5:00 PM on August 1 with roughly 40,000 fighters. The approaching Soviet Army halted on the opposite bank and waited. Stalin also denied Allied planes permission to use Soviet airfields for supply drops for weeks. An estimated 200,000 civilians were killed; survivors were expelled and the city was systematically demolished.

events.title: Stonehenge Completed
events.blurb: Over the course of a millennium, Neolithic builders on a chalk plain in southern England erected a circular arrangement of massive standing stones — some weighing 25 tonnes, dragged from quarries over 250 kilometres away — fitted together with mortise-and-tenon joints as if they were timber. The monument aligns with the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset. Its precise purpose — ritual, astronomical, funerary — has been debated for centuries.
events.revealBlurb: c. 2000 BCE — main sarsen-circle completion on Salisbury Plain. The smaller "bluestones," of volcanic rock, came from the Preseli Hills in Wales. Construction had begun about 5,000 years ago in earthen-bank form. The monument predates the druids by 2,000 years, despite the misattribution.

events.title: St. Paul's Cathedral Completed
events.blurb: After 35 years of construction replacing a medieval cathedral destroyed in the Great Fire of London, a 68-year-old English architect watched his son install the final piece of his new cathedral's lantern atop its dome — the first cathedral anywhere in the world to have been entirely designed, built, and completed by a single architect within his own lifetime. The triple-domed design, inspired by St. Peter's in Rome, rose 111 metres above the City of London.
events.revealBlurb: 1710 — Sir Christopher Wren. He also designed 52 other London churches after the Great Fire of 1666. He was buried in the cathedral's crypt when he died in 1723 at 90; his memorial reads "Si monumentum requiris, circumspice" — if you seek his monument, look around you.

events.title: Chrysler Building Completed
events.blurb: A 319-metre Manhattan skyscraper, topped with a radiator-cap-inspired sunburst spire, opened at the corner of 42nd Street and Lexington Avenue as the tallest building in the world. Its automotive-magnate patron had kept the spire a construction secret; it was assembled inside the tower's upper levels and then hoisted into place in 90 minutes, triumphing over a rival bank project down Wall Street that had briefly claimed the height title. The Empire State Building eclipsed it 11 months later.
events.revealBlurb: May 27, 1930 — architect William Van Alen for Walter Chrysler. The Art Deco ornamentation includes eagle gargoyles at the 61st floor and a 1,700-square-metre ceiling mural in the lobby. Van Alen was never paid his fee — Chrysler accused him of taking bribes from suppliers.

events.title: Golden Gate Bridge Opens
events.blurb: A 2,737-metre suspension bridge painted international orange opened across a strait connecting San Francisco Bay to the Pacific Ocean. At the time the longest suspension span in the world (1,280 metres between its towers), it had been built through the Depression with labour recruited off bread lines and union halls. Workers wore (then-innovative) hard hats and safety harnesses; a net slung below the deck saved 19 men who fell, dubbed the "Halfway to Hell Club."
events.revealBlurb: May 27, 1937 — engineer Joseph Strauss, architect Irving Morrow. 200,000 people walked across on opening day. The famous "international orange" color is maintained by a full-time crew of 38 painters. Bridge suicides have been an anguishing running tally; a suicide barrier was finally completed in 2024.

events.title: Channel Tunnel Opens
events.blurb: A 50-kilometre twin-bore railway tunnel under the English Channel opened, linking France to Britain below the sea floor for the first time in 8,000 years. The tunnel had been proposed repeatedly since the early 19th century but had always been shelved on defensive grounds; the end of the Cold War and European integration finally made it buildable. Construction had involved eleven tunnel-boring machines drilling simultaneously from both sides; the breakthrough was within 35 centimetres alignment.
events.revealBlurb: May 6, 1994 — Queen Elizabeth II and President François Mitterrand cut a ribbon jointly. Total project cost: £9 billion, roughly 80 percent over budget. The tunnel is used by Eurostar passenger trains and the freight-carrying Shuttle. Trains reach 160 km/h underground.

events.title: First Soviet Atomic Bomb Test
events.blurb: Four years after U.S. weapons ended the Pacific war, Soviet scientists detonated their own plutonium implosion device at a test range in the Kazakh steppe. Western intelligence had predicted the breakthrough was at least five years away. The explosion ended the American nuclear monopoly and opened the arms race.
events.revealBlurb: August 29, 1949 — codename RDS-1, nicknamed "First Lightning." The design was largely cribbed from the U.S. Fat Man bomb via spy networks inside the Manhattan Project. Klaus Fuchs had handed over detailed blueprints.

events.title: SALT I Signed
events.blurb: In the ornate Vladimir Hall of the Kremlin, the leaders of the two superpowers signed the first treaty limiting strategic nuclear weapons. It froze the number of intercontinental and submarine-launched ballistic missiles on each side at then-current levels and restricted anti-missile defenses. Neither arsenal shrank, but the race for ever more warheads finally acquired guardrails.
events.revealBlurb: May 26, 1972 — Nixon and Brezhnev in Moscow. The ABM Treaty signed the same day restricted each side to two (later one) missile defense sites. The US withdrew from it in 2002 under George W. Bush.

events.title: Helsinki Accords
events.blurb: Thirty-five nations — every European country except tiny Albania, plus the U.S. and Canada — signed a sweeping final act in the Finnish capital that acknowledged post-war borders while binding signatories to respect human rights. Critics called it a sellout to Moscow. In fact, its human rights provisions gave eastern dissidents a legal framework that would undermine the regimes a decade later.
events.revealBlurb: August 1, 1975 — the "Third Basket" on human rights proved subversive. Czech dissidents founded Charter 77 using its language; the Moscow Helsinki Group followed. Brezhnev didn't realize he'd just signed his system's eventual death warrant.

events.title: Tiananmen Square Protests
events.blurb: For seven weeks, student demonstrators occupied the vast plaza at the heart of the Chinese capital, demanding democratic reforms, press freedom, and an end to official corruption. Their ranks swelled into the hundreds of thousands. Then the government declared martial law, rolled tanks into the city, and cleared the square overnight, killing hundreds or thousands of civilians in the streets around it.
events.revealBlurb: June 4, 1989 — the crackdown. The iconic image of a lone man stopping a column of tanks was taken on June 5 from a hotel balcony. His identity remains unknown. The topic is still heavily censored inside China.

events.title: German Reunification
events.blurb: On a crisp autumn evening, a huge black, red, and gold flag was raised in front of the Reichstag building as the East German state ceased to exist and its 16 million citizens became part of the unified federal republic. Forty-five years of partition, imposed by four occupying armies, ended at the stroke of midnight. Crowds sang the national anthem for the first time as one country.
events.revealBlurb: October 3, 1990 — the date is now German Unity Day. The integration cost West Germany over €2 trillion over three decades. Many eastern cities still empty out; many western taxpayers still grumble about the "solidarity surcharge."

events.title: Charlemagne Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A Frankish king, in a papal basilica in the old western imperial capital for Christmas Mass, rose from prayer to be unexpectedly crowned "Emperor of the Romans" by the pope. The coronation resurrected, at least in title, a western empire that had been extinct for 324 years, and established a relationship between popes and emperors that would shape European politics for eight centuries.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 800 — Charlemagne in Rome, crowned by Pope Leo III. Charlemagne later claimed he had been surprised — but the pope probably wouldn't have dared without his consent. The Holy Roman Empire survived in one form or another until 1806.

events.title: First Crusade Takes Jerusalem
events.blurb: After a month-long siege and a three-year, 3,000-kilometre march from Europe, an army of Frankish knights and footsoldiers breached the walls of a holy city in the Levant and slaughtered its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants indiscriminately over two days — perhaps 30,000 people. The first crusader state was established with a European dynasty on the throne; it would last 88 years.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 1099 — the siege was broken when two Flemish knights scaled a siege tower onto the wall. The leaders competed to be the first to reach the Holy Sepulchre. Godfrey of Bouillon refused the crown of a city "where his savior had worn a crown of thorns" — he was titled "Defender" instead.

events.title: Saladin Retakes Jerusalem
events.blurb: A Kurdish Muslim sultan, having crushed a Crusader field army three months earlier at the Horns of Hattin, accepted the peaceful surrender of the holy city from its desperate defenders after an eight-day siege. In contrast to the bloody Frankish sack of the city 88 years earlier, he permitted ransomed Christians to leave with their possessions and freed many who could not pay. News of the fall triggered the Third Crusade.
events.revealBlurb: October 2, 1187 — Saladin. His reputation for chivalry, magnified by his later adversary Richard the Lionheart, made him a hero of medieval European literature despite being its opponent. Dante placed him in Limbo rather than Hell.

events.title: Joan of Arc Burned at the Stake
events.blurb: A 19-year-old French woman, captured by Burgundian allies of the English and sold to the English crown for 10,000 livres, was tried for heresy by a church court and burned to death in a market square of a Norman city. Her executioners dug through the embers to prove she had died rather than escaped. Her remains were thrown into the Seine. She was canonized by the Vatican 489 years later.
events.revealBlurb: May 30, 1431 — Rouen. A retrial in 1456 cleared her of all charges. The principal heresy she had refused to recant was wearing men's clothes. She became a Catholic saint in 1920 — six years after French troops carried her image into the trenches of World War I.

events.title: Fall of Constantinople
events.blurb: An Ottoman sultan, 21 years old, directed a 53-day siege of the Byzantine capital with 80,000 troops, an army of miners who tunneled under the walls, and enormous bronze cannons that fired 550-kilogram stone balls. The last Roman emperor died fighting at a breach in his city's walls. The 1,100-year-old Byzantine state, the direct legal continuation of Roman rule, ended.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1453 — Mehmed II. The city's Greek name, Constantinople, stayed in formal Ottoman use until 1930; "Istanbul" is how Byzantine Greeks had always said "to the city" colloquially. Hagia Sophia became a mosque that Friday.

events.title: The Rigveda Is Composed
events.blurb: Across the Punjab river plains, priestly families called the rishis composed hymns to deities of fire, storm, soma, and dawn, passing them orally from teacher to student with astonishing precision — no written word, just breath and memory. The result was a corpus of 1,028 hymns in 10,552 verses that survives almost perfectly today: the oldest substantial text in any Indo-European language, and the basis of all subsequent Sanskrit literature.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1200 BCE — composed in the Sapta Sindhu (seven rivers) region. Transmitted entirely by memory for at least a millennium before being written down. The oral tradition was so exacting that modern linguistics uses it to reconstruct the pronunciation of proto-Indo-European, a language no one has ever heard.

events.title: Alexander's Army Crosses into Punjab
events.blurb: A Macedonian king who had already conquered Persia crossed the Hindu Kush and entered the Indus valley, accepting the submission of Taxila before meeting his most formidable Indian opponent at the Jhelum River. King Porus arrived with war elephants, cavalry, and infantry to contest the crossing. Impressed by Porus's defiance even in defeat, Alexander returned the kingdom to him — then turned back west when his exhausted army refused to march further east.
events.revealBlurb: 326 BCE — Battle of the Hydaspes (Jhelum). When Alexander asked how Porus wished to be treated, the king replied, "As a king treats another king." Alexander obliged. Within a decade, Chandragupta Maurya would sweep the remaining Macedonian garrisons from the very ground Alexander had crossed.

events.title: Ashoka Conquers Kalinga
events.blurb: A Mauryan emperor's army conquered a fiercely resistant coastal kingdom after a war that, by the emperor's own inscriptions, killed 100,000 people and displaced 150,000 more. Revolted by the carnage he had ordered, the emperor publicly renounced war, embraced a philosophy of non-violence, and had pillars erected across his realm inscribed with edicts of compassion — the earliest dateable Indian texts we can read today.
events.revealBlurb: c. 261 BCE — Ashoka the Great, Maurya dynasty. The lion capital from his pillar at Sarnath — four lions standing back to back — is now India's national emblem.

events.title: Guru Arjan Dev Is Executed by Mughal Order
events.blurb: The fifth Sikh Guru, who had compiled the Adi Granth and built the Golden Temple, was arrested by the Mughal emperor on charges of blessing a rebel prince. Ordered to pay a fine of 200,000 rupees and alter his scripture's hymns, he refused both. He was then tortured over several days — made to sit on a burning iron plate while red-hot sand was poured over his body — and died in Lahore. His execution permanently changed the relationship between the Sikh Panth and Mughal power.
events.revealBlurb: May 30, 1606 CE — Guru Arjan Dev Ji, Lahore, Mughal Empire under Jahangir. His martyrdom led his successor, Guru Hargobind, to take up two swords — one of spiritual authority, one of temporal power — and build an armed Sikh army.

events.title: The Marathas Are Defeated at the Third Battle of Panipat
events.blurb: A Maratha army of 45,000 soldiers and 200,000 camp followers — including families who had brought their children on what they expected to be a triumphant northern campaign — faced an Afghan force under the Durrani king. After an eight-month standoff that left the Marathas starving, they were crushed in a single morning. Between 60,000 and 70,000 troops died in the battle; up to 40,000 prisoners were massacred the following day.
events.revealBlurb: January 14, 1761 — Ahmad Shah Durrani vs. Sadashivrao Bhau, Panipat. Fought on the same plain as two earlier world-changing battles. The Maratha defeat ended Hindu imperial ambitions and opened India to British expansion. It is said that barely a family in the Deccan was not in mourning afterward.

events.title: Johnstown Flood
events.blurb: After days of heavy rain, a poorly maintained earth dam built to create a private lake for a Pennsylvania hunting club gave way, releasing 20 million tons of water onto the steel-mill town 23 kilometres downstream. The wall of water reached speeds of 65 km/h and was 18 metres high. It killed 2,209 people in 10 minutes.
events.revealBlurb: May 31, 1889 — Johnstown, Pennsylvania. The hunting club's members (including Andrew Carnegie and Henry Clay Frick) were never successfully sued. The flood launched the American Red Cross onto the national stage; Clara Barton ran relief operations for five months.

events.title: San Francisco Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.9 earthquake ripped a 477-kilometre tear through the fault running up the California coast, hitting a West Coast boom city just after 5 AM. The shaking was severe, but the four-day fire that followed — fed by broken gas mains and fought with limited water from shattered pipes — did most of the damage, destroying 80 percent of the city and killing around 3,000.
events.revealBlurb: April 18, 1906 — San Francisco. The mayor authorized dynamiting buildings to create firebreaks; most of the dynamiting actually spread the fire. The opera singer Enrico Caruso, in town for a performance, vowed never to return. He didn't.

events.title: Mount St. Helens Eruption
events.blurb: A Pacific Northwest volcano that had been swelling a grotesque 150-metre bulge on its north flank for two months underwent a catastrophic lateral blast triggered by an earthquake. The collapse produced the largest landslide in recorded history, flattening 600 square kilometres of forest and killing 57 people, including a stubborn innkeeper who refused to evacuate.
events.revealBlurb: May 18, 1980 — Washington State, USA. The innkeeper was Harry R. Truman, 83, who kept pets and a collection of bourbon at his lodge and became a folk hero for his refusal to leave. His body was never found.

events.title: Exxon Valdez Oil Spill
events.blurb: An oil tanker struck a well-charted reef in an Alaskan sound after the captain left the bridge and an inexperienced third mate failed to steer back into the shipping lane. 40,000 tonnes of crude oil gushed into the pristine fjord, ultimately coating 2,100 kilometres of coastline and killing hundreds of thousands of seabirds, sea otters, and orcas.
events.revealBlurb: March 24, 1989 — Prince William Sound, Alaska. The captain, Joseph Hazelwood, had been drinking. It was the worst human-caused environmental disaster in US history until Deepwater Horizon in 2010. Oil is still found under beach gravel in the area today.

events.title: Indian Ocean Tsunami
events.blurb: A magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off the western coast of Sumatra — the third-largest ever recorded — displaced so much water that tsunami waves up to 30 metres high raced across the Indian Ocean, hitting 14 countries within hours. Around 228,000 people died in Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India, Thailand, and as far away as Somalia. No warning system existed.
events.revealBlurb: December 26, 2004 — Boxing Day. A 10-year-old British girl named Tilly Smith recognized the receding tide from a school geography lesson and got her family's Phuket beach evacuated, saving around 100 lives. A basin-wide warning system was operational by 2006.
